nodes.title: Wonder Full unmitigated cybersecurity risk assessment
nodes.statement: Our evaluations put the unmitigated model at “moderate or lower” for both Cybersecurity and Loss of Control before applying our mitigations.

source_refs.locator: §4, PDF p.7, opening paragraph, penultimate sentence

nodes.applicability: Cybersecurity component only; Wonder Full. Loss of Control retained for quotation fidelity, outside analysis.
nodes.argus_reconstruction: Meta assesses unmitigated Wonder Full cybersecurity risk as moderate or lower under its framework. The surrounding mitigated deployment judgment is supporting context, not a second root.

nodes.title: Meaning and scope
nodes.statement: The root is Meta’s cybersecurity baseline-category assessment of Full, under the framework’s catastrophic-risk definition. Its reference to Loss of Control is preserved in the quote but excluded from analysis.

nodes.title: Baseline capability inference
nodes.statement: Capability results are relevant inputs; an inspectable baseline conclusion requires model-specific evidence that no covered cyber scenario receives substantial contribution under plausible elicitation and deployment conditions.

nodes.title: Guarded behavior context
nodes.statement: Six adversarial ASRs provide bounded evidence of refusal robustness and remaining successes. These results qualify deployment context; they do not establish the unmitigated baseline.

nodes.title: Family extension
nodes.statement: Full-based family assessment requires domain-specific capability bounding. Paired launch behavior charts provide limited evidence and show that general capability ordering does not uniformly order refusal, compliance or unauthorized-code results.

nodes.title: Tested-to-served configuration
nodes.statement: Transfer to deployment requires correct model, checkpoint, tool/harness, access and mitigation mapping; Full’s announced route is Muse Code subscribers.

nodes.title: Deployment decision context
nodes.statement: The reported mitigated category and pre-deployment review are consistent with the root, but the public record does not expose the full cyber residual-risk rationale or independent scrutiny.

nodes.title: Continuing assurance
nodes.statement: Monitoring, response, model security and reassessment must preserve the conditions under which deployment risk was judged; their effectiveness is not measured publicly here.

nodes.title: Scenario coverage
nodes.statement: The evaluation suite covers the relevant Cyber 1/2/3 pathways and deployment affordances sufficiently to support the categorical baseline.

nodes.title: Measurement validity
nodes.statement: Capability scoring, intended-task adjudication, elicitation and repeats accurately characterize Full’s relevant capabilities.

nodes.title: Adversarial representativeness
nodes.statement: Robustness tasks, budgets, success criteria and outcomes are informative about relevant misuse attempts.

nodes.title: Family bounding
nodes.statement: Full bounds smaller Wonder’s relevant capabilities in comparable conditions; the inference does not presume weaker models always refuse better.

nodes.title: Serving equivalence
nodes.statement: The tested checkpoint, tools and safeguards map to the served Full configuration and any claimed family deployment.

nodes.title: Decision completeness
nodes.statement: The residual-risk decision integrates relevant favorable and adverse findings, with acceptance criteria and accountable review.

nodes.title: Control persistence
nodes.statement: Cyber monitoring, response and weight protection continue to function as assumed and trigger reassessment when conditions change.

nodes.title: Temporal scope
nodes.statement: The case concerns claims in 14 October captures about the 12 October release; exact release-day text and configuration remain unverified.

nodes.title: Proxy adequacy
nodes.statement: Benchmark success or failure is informative about real threat contribution only under a justified mapping and adequate elicitation.

nodes.title: Scoring adequacy
nodes.statement: Verifier agreement is informative but may share errors; unintended flags must be adjudicated separately from intended exploits.

nodes.title: Attack coverage
nodes.statement: Finite attack portfolios and budgets provide useful but incomplete evidence about adaptive, persistent adversaries.

nodes.title: Cross-variant inference
nodes.statement: A stronger general model can bound some capabilities without necessarily bounding every specialized capability or refusal behavior.

nodes.title: Configuration continuity
nodes.statement: Evaluation configurations and active deployment controls remain comparable across the claimed release scope.

nodes.title: Operational containment
nodes.statement: Layered controls and timely response reduce opportunities for persistent misuse or unauthorized unmitigated access.

nodes.title: Root and surrounding assessment
nodes.statement: Meta assigns the unmitigated model the moderate-or-lower category in cybersecurity. The surrounding paragraph assigns the same category across all domains after mitigation and connects that assessment to deployment.
nodes.applicability: Section introduces Wonder Full as tested model. Only cybersecurity is reconstructed.
nodes.limit: Chemical/biological high-risk uncertainty and Loss of Control are outside the root’s analytic scope. A cyber reduction from high risk is not asserted.

source_refs.locator: §4, PDF p.7, opening paragraph

nodes.title: Family inference
nodes.statement: Meta says results are from its most capable variant, Wonder Full, and on that basis the assessment covers every model in the family.
nodes.applicability: Full test results; extension to smaller Wonder is a publisher inference.
nodes.limit: The card supplies Full’s §4 cyber tests. Launch charts add paired refusal/compliance/security aggregates, but no paired catastrophic-capability assessment or complete family-bounding argument.

nodes.statement: 92 flags captured: 21 via intended vulnerabilities and 71 via unintended vulnerabilities. Meta reports a GPT-cyber verification pass and a separate confirmation using Gemini 3.1 Pro. Only 21 is comparable to the benchmark’s published ranking.
nodes.applicability: Wonder Full; counts of flags, not percentages.
nodes.limit: No total attempted tasks or verifier confusion matrix. The 71 routes show capability and benchmark-validity concerns; they do not establish production compromise or safeguard bypass. A second model verifier is not an independent institutional audit.

nodes.title: Residual assessment and review
nodes.statement: Meta reports extensive evaluations including red teaming across the three framework domains, a mitigated moderate-or-lower residual-risk assessment, and internal governance review before the deployment decision.
nodes.applicability: Publisher’s family-level narrative; not a published cyber-specific decision record.
nodes.limit: No decision date, risk-acceptance worksheet or adverse-result dispositions. No claim of independently verified framework compliance.

nodes.title: External inputs
nodes.statement: Meta reports working with third parties on benchmark development/licensing, threat modeling with outside experts, and engagement with government and other stakeholders.
nodes.applicability: External inputs to catastrophic-risk assessment; cyber-specific evaluator identities and findings not provided here.
nodes.limit: Benchmark provenance, external execution and independent endorsement of the risk judgment are different propositions. None can be substituted for another.

nodes.title: System and evaluation limits
nodes.statement: Meta recommends use-case guardrails and human confirmation for irreversible agent actions; it says testing cannot cover all scenarios and performance varies with serving configuration, quantization, prompts, tools and harness. Not all training languages were evaluated.
nodes.applicability: Family-level cautions relevant to transferring tests to use.
nodes.limit: Recommendations do not prove activation in Muse Code or an API deployment. General coding methodology in §3 does not resolve §4 cyber-specific procedures.

nodes.title: Meaning of risk category
nodes.statement: Moderate or lower permits relevant capabilities while excluding substantial contribution to the defined catastrophic scenarios across plausible development and deployment conditions. High risk concerns substantial contribution; moderate-level mitigation choices depend on tests and deployment strategy.
nodes.applicability: Framework category; substantial contribution means being a material factor in an outcome.
nodes.limit: This is a catastrophic-risk category, not a statement of zero cyber misuse or a numerical safety score. Framework policy is not evidence of Wonder-specific fulfillment.

source_refs.locator: §3.3, Table 1, PDF pp.17–19; Appendix I p.49

nodes.title: Cyber scenario coverage
nodes.statement: Cyber 1 concerns lowered barriers/cost of attacks producing large-scale casualties or significant financial loss; Cyber 2 concerns discovery and reliable exploitation of critical zero-days in popular software; Cyber 3 concerns scaled long-form fraud, extortion and scams.
nodes.applicability: Three outcome families; scenario details are partly withheld by the framework.
nodes.limit: The card’s exploit-focused table alone does not establish coverage of all three or the economic/human baselines.

nodes.title: Cyber operational threshold
nodes.statement: Framework starts with professional offensive tasks relative to human experts, escalates from simple to complex realistic challenges when performance warrants, and uses reliable consistent success for high-risk determinations. Cyber 3 uses bottleneck analysis and deployment-specific evaluations.
nodes.applicability: General decision rule for Cyber 1/2/3.
nodes.limit: No Wonder-specific human comparisons, escalation decision, complex-task outcomes or Cyber 3 results accompany the card’s scores. No universal numeric cutoff is supplied.

nodes.title: Refusals and defensive access policy
nodes.statement: Framework calls for refusal testing, policy scoping to retain defensive uses, monitoring for malicious use, and prompt-injection testing/layered defenses. If the operational threshold is reached it calls for further attacker/defender analysis and system-mitigated reevaluation.
nodes.applicability: Conditional framework commitments; examples include classifiers, rate limits, abuse monitoring, identity controls and logging.
nodes.limit: These examples are not an inventory of controls proven active for Wonder Full. The condition for enhanced cyber measures is not established merely by the chemical/biological result.

nodes.title: Evaluation and governance method
nodes.statement: Framework describes pre-mitigation assessment, context-sensitive elicitation, held-out risk evaluations, repeat evaluations near training completion, mitigation adequacy review, residual threat modeling and deployment approval roles.
nodes.applicability: General process, with deployment context, scaffolding and model security included.
nodes.limit: No Wonder-specific execution logs, evaluation-awareness audit, holdout audit or repetitions are provided by these commitments.

nodes.title: Disclosure commitments and reasons
nodes.statement: Preparedness reports are to explain methods, elicitation/resources/access, risk rationale, mitigation adequacy, adverse behaviors and governance; material changes trigger updates. Framework explicitly withholds constituent threat steps while balancing transparency/security, and permits some report redactions with reasons where feasible.
nodes.applicability: Disclosure policy and explicit framework-level withholding reason.
nodes.limit: No deadline beyond timely deployment-linked reporting is specified. Do not assert a policy breach or infer that the same reason explains absent Wonder denominators, report timing or decision details.

nodes.title: Launch routes
nodes.statement: Wonder is announced on Meta Model API and Muse Code; Wonder Full is announced for Muse Code subscribers. Wonder-powered Muse experiences are described as forthcoming, first for subscribers.
nodes.applicability: Distinct named models and launch routes; corroborated by P4-SRC-004 Takeaways.
nodes.limit: Full API access and completed Muse rollout are not established. No per-route tested checkpoint/control manifest appears.

nodes.title: Weight protection and continuing review
nodes.statement: Card reports lifecycle weight-security measures. Framework describes incident response (p.13), baseline weight controls (p.30), cyber misuse monitoring (p.32), and updates/reassessment (pp.11,46–47).
nodes.applicability: One Wonder-family implementation assertion plus general continuing-control commitments.
nodes.limit: No public Wonder Full operational effectiveness metrics, security audit, incident denominators or response-latency results in this corpus.

nodes.title: Baseline threshold and scenario coverage
nodes.statement: No Full-specific audit trail maps capability results, human/cost baselines, escalation decisions and Cyber 1/2/3 coverage to the moderate-or-lower determination.
nodes.observed: Three capability headline scores are public; framework requires scenario-sensitive cyber judgments, including scaled scams.
nodes.closure_evidence: A sanitized scenario-to-test matrix, human/no-model baselines, elicitation bounds, simple-to-complex escalation rationale, complex challenge and Cyber 3 results, uncertainty analysis and dated criterion-by-criterion adjudication. A defensible qualitative rule is sufficient; a numeric universal cutoff is not demanded.
nodes.alternative_interpretation: Meta may have fuller internal evaluations supporting the category. High benchmark performance alone neither proves nor disproves substantial contribution to catastrophic outcomes.
nodes.omission_reason: Framework p.20 expressly withholds constituent threat steps to balance transparency/security. That reason is known only for those details; the reason for missing Wonder aggregate mappings and adjudication is UNKNOWN_REASON.

nodes.title: Capability measurement and ExploitGym validity
nodes.statement: Public capability results lack exact checkpoint/mitigation state, task and trial denominators, harness/budget/version information, uncertainty, human baselines and independently inspectable verification of intended versus unintended routes.
nodes.observed: Meta discloses the 21/71 split and two-model verification, a useful correction to the 92-flag headline.
nodes.closure_evidence: A safe method manifest for each benchmark, task counts and per-task outcomes, repetitions/seeds, scoring/aggregation rules, elicitation and safeguard state; a sanitized 92-flag adjudication ledger with independent expert sample review and sensitivity to unintended solves. No exploit recipes are needed.
nodes.alternative_interpretation: Unintended routes may reflect meaningful discovery skill while invalidating intended-task scoring. Removing them from the comparable count does not erase their capability significance; including them as intended successes is unjustified.
nodes.omission_reason: UNKNOWN_REASON for missing method details and adjudication records.

nodes.title: Robustness denominators and adverse-result disposition
nodes.statement: No public denominators, attempts/budgets, success rubrics, uncertainty, attack construction, safeguard stack, severity adjudication or remediation/retest accounting permits a deployment-risk interpretation of the nonzero successes.
nodes.observed: CyberBench 0.8/0.8, PolyGuard cyber 1.1/2.3, RedCode 9.0/8.0 are ASR percentages for separate single/multi-turn setups. Launch charts separately report 96.9% Full misuse refusal, 93.3% defensive compliance and 10.7% unauthorized-code ASR.
nodes.closure_evidence: Per-setup task/objective/query counts and attempts, stopping rules, attack budgets, languages, judge validation and intervals; sanitized successful-output utility/severity classes, fixes and retests; separate benign-task false refusals and end-to-end adversarial task results.
nodes.alternative_interpretation: Some scored successes may have little operational usefulness, while persistent actors may exploit successful objectives across sessions. The aggregates cannot distinguish these possibilities. Complements of ASR are not automatically refusal rates.
nodes.omission_reason: UNKNOWN_REASON; no Wonder-specific omission explanation found.

nodes.title: Full-to-Wonder family inference
nodes.statement: Paired behavioral aggregates are public, but no paired catastrophic-capability evaluations, matched-test method manifest or domain-specific argument establishes that Full bounds smaller Wonder across the cybersecurity assessment and deployment contexts.
nodes.observed: The publisher expressly bases family assessment on its most capable variant, Full. Launch charts supply limited paired behavioral results: Full/Wonder refusal 96.9/93.7%, defensive compliance 93.3/94.5%, unauthorized-code ASR 10.7/10.5%.
nodes.closure_evidence: A variant/checkpoint matrix, paired capability and robustness tests with matched harness/budget, explanation of relevant training/serving differences, and a documented bounding argument with exceptions and uncertainty.
nodes.alternative_interpretation: Full may conservatively bound offensive capability, but specialized behavior and refusal robustness need not order the same way. This gap limits the family extension, not the identity of the Full root.

nodes.title: Test-to-deployment and mitigation mapping
nodes.statement: No dated matrix maps cyber tests to actual served checkpoints, tools, permissions, system policies, classifiers, rate limits or other controls per route. The cyber stack cannot be inferred from the paragraph’s chemical/biological classifier example.
nodes.observed: Full is announced for Muse Code subscribers; smaller Wonder is on API and Muse Code. Card recommends added guardrails and reports mitigated assessment.
nodes.closure_evidence: Versioned Full Muse Code serving attestation and test-to-route mapping, control defaults/availability and change history; separate smaller-Wonder API/Code rows and any later Muse rollout; targeted comparative tests or an independent configuration audit.
nodes.alternative_interpretation: Common infrastructure could make tests representative, but the public documents do not establish it. Recommended deployer guardrails may differ from Meta’s active product controls.
nodes.omission_reason: UNKNOWN_REASON; launch-route distinction itself is public and established.

nodes.title: Residual-risk rationale, review and independent scrutiny
nodes.statement: The public corpus lacks the detailed cyber decision rationale, treatment of residual successes, acceptance criteria, dated accountable review and independently authored assessment connecting tests and deployment conditions.
nodes.observed: Card reports a mitigated moderate-or-lower assessment and internal governance review; third-party inputs are described. Separate full report not located in the bounded search.
nodes.closure_evidence: The promised report or equivalent inspectable cyber case summary, a dated decision record by accountable role, criterion-to-evidence links including adverse results and uncertainty, and independently authored evaluation/audit findings with access, funding and editorial-control disclosure. A report alone narrows the gap only to the extent it supplies the missing evidence.
nodes.alternative_interpretation: The internal record may be complete. Nonzero ASR need not contradict moderate catastrophic risk; private external review may exist. No report-publication deadline breach is inferred.
nodes.omission_reason: Report status: NOT_LOCATED_IN_BOUNDED_PUBLIC_SEARCH as of 2026-10-14. Publication timing and document-specific omissions: UNKNOWN_REASON. General redaction policy does not explain each omission.

nodes.title: Continuing control and weight-security effectiveness
nodes.statement: No Wonder Full-specific operational evidence establishes misuse detection, intervention latency, monitoring coverage, security-control effectiveness or reassessment triggers in practice.
nodes.observed: The card reports lifecycle weight security; framework describes monitoring, incident response and update mechanisms.
nodes.closure_evidence: Privacy-preserving monitoring/response metrics with denominators and observation windows, blinded detection exercises, security audit summary, change/incident escalation criteria and dated follow-up assessments. Given the two-day launch interval, later evidence may be needed; no historical incident-free record is presumed.
nodes.alternative_interpretation: Controls may work effectively despite sparse early public telemetry. No observed incident or control failure is established by this gap.
nodes.omission_reason: UNKNOWN_REASON for unavailable implementation/effectiveness records; short observation period limits possible empirical evidence.
